title: Magnetic anomalies over ocean ridges and moving plates
summary: F. J. Vine and D. H. Matthews's 1963 Nature paper, "Magnetic Anomalies Over Oceanic Ridges," interpreted the striped magnetic anomalies parallel to mid-ocean ridges. New crust form
body: F. J. Vine and D. H. Matthews's 1963 Nature paper, "Magnetic Anomalies Over Oceanic Ridges," interpreted the striped magnetic anomalies parallel to mid-ocean ridges. New crust formed at a ridge records the Earth's magnetic field as it cools, and the field reverses from time to time, so the stripes are a tape of those reversals if the seafloor spreads. That pattern was a decisive piece of evidence for seafloor spreading. The U.S. Geological Survey's This Dynamic Earth states the resulting theory: the Earth's outermost layer is fragmented into a dozen or more large and small plates that move relative to one another as they ride atop hotter material. The 1963 paper is the magnetic argument. The USGS page is a later official summary of the plate picture. Neither source is a measurement of every plate's present speed.
